reader.title: Killing of Harry Wheeler
bases: After an inquest charged him with killing Thomas Phillips, a warrant was issued and a posse, with a constable, pursued Harry Wheeler and shot him dead at Lacroix's Ferry on Little river (A6, A7).

A posse shot Wheeler to death for the killing of Phillips (A6, A7), and a Natchitoches paper called it 'the justice meted to him that we predicted' while a Montgomery correspondent wrote that every pursuer would have killed him 'upon sight' (A4, A3); the killers' defenders, however, say the posse acted on a warrant and fired only when he fled armed, so whether the killing was without lawful authority rests on their account alone (A6).

The Natchitoches Vindicator, the Natchitoches Register and the Montgomery citizens' letter independently report that pursuers killed Wheeler on Little river (A4, A7, A6); what is disputed is the death of his wife and the exact circumstances, not the killing itself (A1, A7).

summary.text: The killing of Harry Wheeler was the shooting of a Black cropper by a posse at Lacroix's Ferry on Little river, in the eastern end of Grant Parish, Louisiana, about July 13, 1880.
Wheeler had been accused of killing his employer, Thomas Phillips, a week earlier, and he was shot dead while the posse tried to take him.

The case drew a three-week exchange in the Louisiana press after the paper We The People reported that Grant Parish citizens had killed both Wheeler and his wife, a charge the Colfax Chronicle called a slander.
Wheeler worked as a cropper on Phillips's plantation about five miles from Montgomery and was in debt to him.
According to the Colfax Chronicle, the two men fell out when Wheeler's wife wanted to hire one of her sons to a neighbor and Phillips objected, "claiming a right to the services of the whole family."
On July 6, the Chronicle said, the wife berated Phillips near a branch by his house, and when he picked up a switch and started toward her, Wheeler shot him in the back of the head.
An inquest held by S. C. Curry, justice of the peace for ward 7, found that Phillips died of a wound from a shotgun "in the hands of Harry Wheeler," and a warrant was issued.
When the officer holding the warrant could not find Wheeler, a posse searched the country as he made his way through the woods toward the Mississippi.

According to a letter signed by eight Montgomery citizens, the posse surrounded him at Lacroix's Ferry a week after the shooting; he drew a knife and ran with a shotgun, and men posted nearby fired, "shooting him through body and brain."

The Natchitoches Register gave a different scene: a ferryman pointed out the abandoned house where Wheeler was hiding, the constable and posse surrounded it, and Wheeler rushed out with a shotgun and was killed when he did not surrender.
The Natchitoches Vindicator reported that his body was "fairly riddled with bullets" and buried where he fell.
The justice of the peace for ward 2 held an inquest, and the body was buried near the ferry; no inquest verdict is reported.

No action against the posse appears in the coverage; instead, a Montgomery correspondent signing as "M. A. D." told those who killed Wheeler, "Gentlemen, you did your duty, and the people will stand by you."

Only white papers covered the killing, all of them in Louisiana, and most coverage came in response to a now-missing account in We The People that the Colfax Chronicle denounced as "a lie out of the whole cloth."

The Chronicle, published in Grant Parish, answered with an editorial on August 7, a correspondent's letter on August 14, and the citizens' letter, "A Slander Refuted," on August 21, which called the proceedings "by authority, legal and deliberate" and rejected any "bloody shirt outrage."
Those rebuttals spread through reprints in the Louisiana Democrat of Alexandria on August 18 and in the People's Vindicator of Natchitoches and the Louisiana Capitolian on August 28.

The Natchitoches papers framed the killing as earned punishment: the Vindicator, as quoted by the Donaldsonville Chief, called it "the justice meted to him that we predicted," and the Register's report ran in the St. Landry Democrat as "A Murderer Killed."

Elsewhere the episode shrank to one line in the Morehouse Clarion's state news, which said only that "a negro murderer" had been overtaken "in Natchitoches" and shot by his pursuers; no Black-press coverage was found.
The fate of Wheeler's wife was the main point of dispute.

We The People, as the Chronicle described it, said the citizens killed her with her husband, and the Register reported that she was found dead after the shooting, "supposed" to have been thrown from her horse, adding that she had earlier said she decoyed Phillips for her husband to kill.

The Chronicle and its Montgomery correspondents insisted she was alive, though they placed her variously on Cane river, on Little river in Natchitoches Parish, and on Col. Thompson's plantation in that parish.
Every account of how Wheeler died comes from the pursuers' side or papers relaying it.

accounts.label: We The People (as described by its critics)
accounts.gist: Reported that the citizens of Grant parish killed both Wheeler and his wife; the paper's own text was not found, and its version is known only from the Colfax Chronicle's rebuttal.

accounts.label: Colfax Chronicle editorial
accounts.gist: Wheeler shot Phillips in the back of the head during a family labor dispute, possibly by arrangement with his wife; he was tracked to Little river and 'shot in attempting to escape'; the wife lives on Cane river.

accounts.label: Montgomery citizens' letter
accounts.gist: After an inquest and warrant, a posse surrounded Wheeler at Lacroix's Ferry a week later; he drew a knife and ran with a shotgun, and parties posted around fired, killing him; an inquest followed and the wife is alive on Col. Thompson's plantation.

accounts.label: Natchitoches Register
accounts.gist: A ferryman showed a constable and posse the abandoned house where Wheeler hid; he rushed out with a shotgun, refused to surrender and was killed; his wife, on horseback, was later found dead, supposedly thrown, and had said she decoyed Phillips.

accounts.label: Natchitoches Vindicator
accounts.gist: Wheeler was overtaken on Little River and received 'the justice' the paper had predicted; his body was riddled with bullets and buried where he fell.

framing.detail: The Colfax Chronicle headed its account 'A Lie and a Slander', called We The People's version 'an infamous and malicious slander' and said the result was 'no more than was to have been expected'.

The Chronicle printed a correspondent's letter telling the killers 'Gentlemen, you did your duty, and the people will stand by you' and a citizens' letter headed 'A Slander Refuted' that called the proceedings legal and dismissed any 'bloody shirt outrage'.
The Natchitoches Vindicator, quoted by the Donaldsonville Chief, called the killing 'the justice meted to him that we predicted'.
The St. Landry Democrat ran the Register's report under 'A Murderer Killed', treating the accusation as fact, and the Morehouse Clarion gave a single line on a 'negro murderer'.
The Louisiana Democrat, People's Vindicator and Louisiana Capitolian reprinted the Chronicle's rebuttals.
